title: Splice the Cables
statement: A crew must join several cable pieces into one continuous cable. Joining two pieces of lengths a and b costs a + b units of labor and produces one piece of length a + b. Given the piece lengths in the array lengths, return the minimum total labor needed to join every piece into a single cable. A single piece or no pieces needs no labor.

examples.explanation: Join 2 and 3 for 5, then 4 and 5 for 9, then 6 and 9 for 15. The total is 5 + 9 + 15 = 29, and no other order is cheaper.
One piece is already a single cable.

hints.content: A piece that is joined early gets its length counted in every later join it participates in.
So the longest pieces should be joined as late as possible and the shortest as early as possible.
At each step, join the two shortest pieces currently available.
Repeatedly finding the two smallest pieces by scanning is slow; a min-heap gives them in logarithmic time.
Push the joined piece back so it competes with the remaining pieces in later steps.

testCases.explanation: Join 2 and 3 for 5, then 4 and 5 for 9, then 6 and 9 for 15. The total is 5 + 9 + 15 = 29, and no other order is cheaper.
One piece is already a single cable.
Join into two 20s (cost 40), then 40 (cost 40), for 80 total.
Joining the two 1s first (cost 2) then 2 + 100 (102) then 102 + 100 (202) totals 306.
The greedy order pays 2, 4, 7, 9 and 16 for a total of 38.

solutions.title: Scan for the two shortest pieces each round
solutions.intuition: Joining the two shortest pieces first keeps long pieces out of as many joins as possible, and that greedy choice can be simulated directly.
solutions.approach: While more than one piece remains, sort the pieces, remove the two shortest, add their sum to the labor, and put the joined piece back.
solutions.pseudocode: labor = 0; while more than one piece: sort; joined = first + second; labor += joined; replace the two with joined; return labor.
commonMistakes: Joining pieces left to right in input order, which is not optimal.
Forgetting to put the joined piece back into the pool.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Greedy pairing of the two shortest pieces is optimal by the same exchange argument as optimal merge patterns. Sorting the pool every round works but is slow; a min-heap supports the two removals and one insertion per round in logarithmic time.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For [4, 3, 2, 6], sorting gives [2, 3, 4, 6]; join 2 and 3 for 5, leaving [4, 6, 5].

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Sort to [4, 5, 6]; join 4 and 5 for 9, leaving [6, 9]; join for 15. Total labor 5 + 9 + 15 = 29.

solutions.title: Min-heap of pieces
solutions.intuition: The greedy rule only ever needs the two smallest pieces, which is exactly what a min-heap serves efficiently.
solutions.approach: Push all lengths into a min-heap. While at least two pieces remain, pop the two smallest, add their sum to the labor, and push the sum back.
solutions.pseudocode: heap = all lengths; labor = 0; while heap size > 1: a = pop, b = pop; labor += a + b; push(a + b); return labor.
commonMistakes: Using a max-heap or sorting descending, which pairs the longest pieces first.
Returning the final piece length instead of the accumulated labor.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Each join should combine the two shortest available pieces, because a piece's length is paid again in every later join that includes it. A binary min-heap gives the two smallest in O(log n) each, so n − 1 joins cost O(n log n). I implement the heap by hand since JavaScript has no built-in priority queue.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For [4, 3, 2, 6], the heap yields 2 and 3; labor becomes 5 and 5 is pushed back.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Next it yields 4 and 5; labor becomes 14 and 9 is pushed.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: Finally 6 and 9 are joined for 15, so the labor totals 29.
